reasoning: The tweet describes an Istanbul rally as being 'in support of the Iranian people,' but multiple sources confirm it was a pro-Iranian-regime rally, not a pro-Iranian-people rally. The video is a confirmed 2015 promotional stunt by E! for the TV series 'The Royals,' not real footage of a child escaping Buckingham Palace. This has been debunked by PolitiFact, Snopes, AP News, and Full Fact. The person in the video was not a child.

The claim that Birmingham City Council meetings 'have stopped being conducted in English altogether' is false. Official council meetings are conducted in English, streamed online, and have published minutes in English. The video likely shows an informal community gathering, not an official council meeting.

While Greenland sharks can theoretically live 250-500 years, the claim that a specific shark 'has been alive since 1627' is misleading. The 2016 study used radiocarbon dating on dead specimens to estimate ages between 272-512 years; the exact age of any living shark cannot be precisely determined, and the viral photo's shark was not verified as 392 years old.

The community note claims the video is AI-generated. While I cannot verify the video directly, AI-generated emotional animal rescue videos are a well-documented engagement farming tactic. The note provides supporting references. The emotional framing is typical of synthetic content.

The tweet appears to promote false claims about Alex Pretti being fired from his nursing job. Multiple fact-checkers (Snopes, Lead Stories, IBTimes) have confirmed he was never fired and was employed at the Minneapolis VA Medical Center at the time of his death. The false claim originated from a Vietnamese spam site.

The tweet claims Benny Johnson 'confirmed' $31 billion in homelessness spending was fraudulent. While California has spent tens of billions on homelessness (estimates range $24B-$37B depending on timeframe), Johnson's announced investigation focused on COVID relief fraud and SNAP benefits, not homelessness spending specifically. The attribution of the $31B figure to Johnson's confirmation is misleading.
